newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INSTANT VIEW - Earnings data seen comforting RBNZ.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Earnings data seen comforting RBNZ.

text.p: Following are economists' initial reactions to the New Zealand August Quarterly Employment Survey data released on Tuesday.
Private sector average ordinary time earnings rose 3.7 percent for the year, compared with a consensus forecast of 4.2 percent.
Total average ordinary time earnings rose 3.4 percent against expectations of a 3.5 percent rise.
PAUL STEWART, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK
"I think the results are fairly encouraging, particularly the abatement in the quarterly growth rate of the private sector average hourly earings.
"We were expecting to see a slowdown in wage pressures there but it was slightly softer than we anticipated and I think that will be encouraging for the Reserve Bank.
"It reinforces the view that an easing in policy is likely sometime over the next six months or so, but I wouldn't say anything much beyond that."

He said he would not rule out an easing in December entirely, "but we think the Reserve Bank may be encouraged to wait at least until the December quarter CPI (on January 17), and also clearly they'll want to have a fairly good view about the track for fiscal policy before they commit themselves too much."
HAMISH MACALISTER, WESTPAC ECONOMIST
"Private sector expectations were somewhat over four percent and 3.7 percent was a very good number, and also for the total ordinary time it was very positive to see that had peaked.

"If you put that into unit labour cost terms we'll actually see for the first time since around March 1994 the growth rate in unit labour costs actually turn around which would be very positive from the Reserve Bank's point of view.

"It's the second half of the labour market picture. The labour market was cited as a risk by the bank in the past and we had some strong employment growth, but that was all coming through in part-time jobs rather than full-time jobs so again that was relatively speaking a good number for them.
"Now that they have their wages data as well that is the second half of the picture and they both add up to a good good outlook for the Reserve Bank.
"This, together with a lot of the other data, all the partial indicators that we have had through so far is very positive in terms of the outlook for inflation over the next six to nine months."
ANTHONY BYETT, ASB BANK ECONOMIST
"It's not showing that wages are blowing out of line...(We're) on track basically for an easing over the next six months."
He said there were no major implications for interest rates or the currency at this stage.

"I don't think they (the figures) were that far away from where the Reserve Bank and other economists had been picking them. If anything, maybe just a small rally in interest rates, but nothing huge...
"There's no shock value in it, but enough information to say things are on track and lower interest rates are in the pipeline."
MATTHEW GOODSON, GARLICK AND CO ECONOMIST

"Clearly one of the Reserve Bank's key worries is abating. All the evidence we've seen on the labour market is for weakness -- ANZ job ads, full-time jobs in the Household Labour Force Survey, and now this, and I suspect the Labour Cost Index on Friday will back that up as well. Clearly the labour market is ceasing to be a concern, I think, on the inflationary front."
Goodson said, however, that the wage data tended to jump around on a quarterly basis and he cautioned against reading too much into a single set of figures.

"It fits the scenario that we've been painting quite well in that the economy has weakened. The fact that the hours worked were at the lowest levels since August 1993 was quite significant, as were the lower overtime hours.
"That is consistent with the exporters pulling back on production and import substitution companies struggling a bit with the high Kiwi dollar.
"It fits into the jigsaw nicely in terms of the economy slowing down from about August-September onward. The danger of some wage push inflation is just not there.
"I don't read too much into it other than that it is consistent with the slowing economy. It shows the labour market is certainly not as tight as it was a year ago."
--Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
